candidates.attacker_control: The value of any `@Path`-annotated service-method parameter that the application derives from untrusted input (resource id, username, tenant, file name, version string, etc.). Retrofit converts it to a String and performs no structural validation: `ParameterHandler.Path.apply` only null-checks (ParameterHandler.java:94-98) and `RequestFactory.validatePathName` validates only the compile-time placeholder name, not the runtime value (RequestFactory.java:724-733).
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked and set aside: (a) default `encoded=false` does percent-encode `/` and `%` (RequestBuilder.java:103,127), which narrows but does not eliminate the issue because `.` is never encoded and `..` alone still forms a normalizable segment; (b) `RequestFactory` validates only the placeholder name regex `[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9_-]*` and its presence in the URL (RequestFactory.java:724-733), never the runtime value; (c) `ParameterHandler.Path.apply` only rejects null (ParameterHandler.java:94-98); (d) `RequestBuilder.get()` rejects only a null result from `baseUrl.resolve` (lines 198-201) - a traversal value still yields a valid non-null URL; (e) whole-repo searches for `traversal`, `perform path traversal`, `PATH_TRAVERSAL`, and `%2e` returned no matches, so no hidden guard exists; (f) grep of `@Path` handling shows no caller-side sanitization. Remaining uncertainty is the exact OkHttp dot-segment normalization behavior (dependency source not in snapshot) and whether a given application actually feeds untrusted data into `@Path`.
candidates.impact: Confused-deputy path traversal / endpoint confusion: a crafted `@Path` value causes the app to send a request to a different path than the annotated endpoint on the same host/scheme (e.g. `users/{id}/repos` with id=`..` becomes `users/../repos`; with `encoded=true`, `../../admin` can escape the base path). Because the request is issued by the application with its own credentials/interceptors, path-keyed client-side allow-lists or server-side authorization/routing can be bypassed, wrong API versions or other resources can be addressed, and path-scoped caches/WAF rules can be evaded. It cannot redirect the request to another host via literal dot segments alone.
candidates.prerequisites: (1) A Retrofit service interface with at least one `@Path` parameter whose value is attacker-influenced. (2) For manipulation in the default `encoded=false` mode: the value must be exactly `..` (or `.`) so that it becomes a whole path segment; literal `/` and `%` are percent-encoded in this mode, so slash-separated multi-segment traversal requires (3) `@Path(encoded = true)`, an opt-in documented in Path.java:59-62, where `/` passes through untouched (e.g. `../../admin`). (4) OkHttp's HttpUrl must normalize dot segments when the relative URL is resolved against the base URL; this is the documented resolution semantics referenced by Retrofit.Builder.baseUrl's Javadoc (Retrofit.java:461-519), but the OkHttp 3.11.0 source itself is a dependency and is not in this snapshot.
candidates.root_cause: Retrofit 2.4.x inserts `@Path` values into the endpoint's relative URL with `relativeUrl.replace("{" + name + "}", canonicalizeForPath(value, encoded))` (RequestBuilder.java:89-95). `canonicalizeForPath` (RequestBuilder.java:97-144) percent-encodes only C0/non-ASCII characters, the always-encode set `" \"<>^`{}|\\?#"` (line 33), and `/`/`%` when `alreadyEncoded == false` (lines 103,127). The `.` character is never encoded, and there is no check rejecting `.`/`..`/`%2e` segments before the relative URL is resolved against the base URL in `RequestBuilder.get()` (lines 189-202) / `addQueryParam()` (lines 146-164). OkHttp's `HttpUrl.resolve`/`newBuilder` normalizes dot segments, so the value can change the path structure of the final request. The @Path Javadoc still promises values are 'URL encoded' and used as a 'Named replacement in a URL path segment' (Path.java:28-40), so the contract is broken by dot segments.
candidates.title: @Path parameter values are neither encoded for '.'/'..' nor validated, allowing request-path traversal / endpoint confusion
candidates.trace: Interface invocation -> OkHttpCall.createRawCall (OkHttpCall.java:189-195) -> RequestFactory.create (RequestFactory.java:92-114) -> ParameterHandler.Path.apply (ParameterHandler.java:94-100) -> RequestBuilder.addPathParam (RequestBuilder.java:89-95) -> canonicalizeForPath (97-144; '.' passes through the fast and slow paths) -> substituted relativeUrl -> RequestBuilder.get()/addQueryParam resolves it with baseUrl.resolve(relativeUrl) (line 197) or baseUrl.newBuilder(relativeUrl) (line 149) and build() (line 193), where OkHttp collapses/skips dot segments and the final okhttp3.Request is created (lines 226-228).
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed; no tests or code were executed. Exploitability depends on an application passing attacker-controlled values into `@Path` and (for multi-segment traversal) on `encoded=true`. OkHttp's dot-segment normalization during `HttpUrl.resolve`/`newBuilder` is assumed from the documented `baseUrl` resolution semantics (Retrofit.java:461-519) because the OkHttp 3.11.0 dependency source is outside the snapshot. Server-side effect depends on the backend's routing and authorization.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-22 Improper Limitation of a Pathname (URL path traversal via unvalidated/incompletely-encoded path segment values)

coverage_summary: Model-visible scope is 196 files (no binaries/symlinks/sensitive-path exclusions; same filters for B0/P1). The P1 relation index reports complete indexing of all 196 files (1,187 symbols, 2,005 calls, 1,685 edges) with no missing files and no SAST/runtime oracle; its CALLS/CONTAINS/CALL_SITE edges around `RequestBuilder.addPathParam` and `canonicalizeForPath` were used only for navigation and were verified in source text. I deep-read the core request-construction path (RequestBuilder, ParameterHandler, RequestFactory, OkHttpCall, HttpServiceMethod, Retrofit, Platform, BuiltInConverters, Utils, ExecutorCallAdapterFactory, CompletableFutureCallAdapterFactory, DefaultCallAdapterFactory, OptionalConverterFactory, Response, Invocation) and spot-checked converters (Gson, Moshi, Jackson, protobuf, JAXB, SimpleXML), adapters (RxJava/RxJava2/Guava), and retrofit-mock. Not read line-by-line: most http/* annotation files, several adapter/converter modules (scalars, wire, java8/guava optional, scala, remaining RxJava files), package-info files, all samples, website assets, and build/CI scripts. Build/tests were not executed.
limitations: No code was compiled or executed; all conclusions are static source reading. The OkHttp 3.11.0 dependency (including HttpUrl.resolve/newBuilder dot-segment normalization) is not in the snapshot, so its behavior is inferred from Retrofit's documented baseUrl resolution semantics (Retrofit.java:461-519).

Exploitability is deployment-dependent: it requires an application to source a `@Path` argument from untrusted input; with default `encoded=false` only a bare `..`/`.` segment is usable, while full multi-segment traversal needs `@Path(encoded = true)`.
P1 relation index is syntactic/navigation-only; it neither proves data flow nor reachability, and files not read line-by-line (listed in coverage) are not claimed to have been reviewed.
The server-side consequence (which endpoint is reached and whether it exposes data or performs privileged actions) cannot be determined from this repository.

rejected_leads.reason: By design (RequestFactory.java:319-350): a full or relative URL supplied to @Url is the caller's explicit choice. No encoding/validation bypass relative to the library contract, and no attacker control unless the application chooses to pass untrusted data; not a source-evidenced defect of this snapshot.

@Header/@HeaderMap delegate to okhttp3.Request.Builder.addHeader (RequestBuilder.java:77-87), which validates names/values; @Field/@FieldMap go through okhttp3.FormBody.add/addEncoded (RequestBuilder.java:166-173). No local bypass of those checks found in the snapshot.

JaxbResponseConverter explicitly disables external entities and DTDs (JaxbResponseConverter.java:37-39). SimpleXML/Wire/Protobuf response converters contain no source evidence of unsafe parser configuration; not verified further.

summary: Retrofit (2.4.1-SNAPSHOT, okhttp 3.11.0) source snapshot. The strongest source-backed candidate is missing dot-segment handling for `@Path` parameter values: `RequestBuilder.addPathParam` substitutes the value into the method's relative URL after only percent-encoding a fixed character set, never encoding or rejecting `.`/`..` (or `%2e`) path segments; the substituted URL is then resolved against the base URL, where dot segments are normalized away. An application that fills a `@Path` parameter from untrusted input can therefore be induced to request a different path than the annotated endpoint, within the same host. No other candidate reached this evidence level.
